headline: Reddit uses AI to combat AI-generated spam on its platform, blocking millions of views daily
summary: Reddit's new LLM-powered systems block 23 million spam views and nearly 2 million inauthentic votes daily, reducing user exposure to spam by 20% since January 2026.
details: Reddit is now deploying its own AI tools, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs), to combat the surge of AI-generated content and spam across its platform. These automated systems have been highly effective, blocking 23 million spam views and catching approximately 25,000 posts and comments daily.

The platform also reports revoking close to two million inauthentic votes each day. As a result of these measures, users experienced a 20 percent reduction in spam exposure from January to March 2026 compared to the previous quarter.

Reddit utilizes LLMs to detect suspicious activity from the moment an account is created, identifying subtle, coordinated fake behaviors and artificial hype. An additional layer of protection forces "fishy automated accounts" to verify their humanity.

Beyond just AI-generated 'slop,' these new enforcement actions also target hate and violence in all English text content, with plans to expand to more languages. The time from detection to enforcement has been cut to less than five seconds, reducing user exposure to harmful content by over 40 percent.

This move marks a significant step for Reddit, which has had a complex relationship with AI, including past incidents like researchers conducting experiments with AI-generated comments. Last year, Reddit also introduced a new licensing protocol to compensate for AI companies scraping its data.

Despite these challenges, Reddit has embraced AI on its own terms, as demonstrated by the introduction of its Reddit Answers search feature. The platform continues to leverage AI to improve its user experience and maintain content integrity.

headline_marked: [[Google Chrome Installed a 4GB AI Model]] on Your PC
headline: Google Chrome Installed a 4GB AI Model on Your PC
summary: Google's Gemini Nano AI model, a 4GB file, has been found automatically installed in Chrome folders on many PCs. Users report it re-downloads even after manual deletion, raising privacy concerns.
details: A 4GB file named 'weights.bin', identified as Google's Gemini Nano on-device AI model, has been discovered deep within Chrome's browser folders on users' computers. This installation reportedly occurred without any user consent or notification.

Swedish privacy researcher Alexander Hanff first uncovered this by analyzing macOS kernel logs, with the same phenomenon later confirmed on Windows and Linux systems. Google internally refers to the folder containing the model as 'OptGuideOnDeviceModel', a name Hanff suggests is deliberately ambiguous.

Chrome automatically checks hardware specifications, including GPU tier, CPU core count, 16GB+ RAM, and 22GB+ free storage. If a machine meets these criteria, the model is downloaded in the background, typically completing within 14 minutes, without any user prompt.

Even if users manually delete the 'weights.bin' file, restarting Chrome triggers an automatic re-download. The browser treats the deletion as a temporary error, attempting to restore it at the next opportunity, with some users reporting multiple versions accumulating to over 12GB.

Google describes Gemini Nano as a "lightweight on-device model" and states that an "On-Device AI" toggle under Settings > System began rolling out in February 2026 to allow users to disable it. However, many users, including Hanff, have not yet received this toggle and must resort to manual flag or registry edits.

The on-device Gemini Nano powers features like Help Me Write, phishing and scam detection, tab group suggestions, and page summarization. Google highlights that local processing enables real-time threat detection for phishing sites that exist for very short durations, which cloud-based systems might miss.

Google's justification for on-device processing is enhanced privacy, as no data is sent to Google's servers. While this logic holds for the features themselves, the installation process raises significant questions.

Critics argue that installing a 4GB AI model without explicit user consent violates Article 5(3) of the EU's ePrivacy Directive, which mandates "freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous consent" for storing information on a user's device. This is the same principle behind cookie banners.
